name: PT Batavia Prosperindo Internasional Tbk

frontmatter.title: Batavia Prosperindo Internasional: a good franchise at a growth-stock price
frontmatter.summary: BPII owns a top-tier Indonesian asset manager, a vehicle-leasing business and a motor-heavy general insurer. The franchise is real, but the shares trade at a premium book multiple for a group earning below its cost of equity while nine-month profit has almost halved on motor underwriting losses. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: BPAM is the group quality asset: seventh in the OJK investment-manager table, the highest Pefindo manager rating, and AUM of 56.4 IDR tntn at September 2026 [S4][S7].
The near-term earnings driver is negative: nine-month net profit to the parent fell to 62.6 IDR bnbn from 111 IDR bnbn as motor insurance swung to an underwriting loss of 41.8 IDR bnbn [S5].
The market still pays 2.7x book for a group whose sustainable ROE we place below its cost of equity; our justified P/BV is 0.6x [S2].

The discount is not closable by arithmetic: a 10.1% free float and IDR21.4m average daily turnover put the stock in the deepest band of the house liquidity schedule, which fixes the target haircut rather than leaving it to judgement [S0].
The dividend held near the prior level is the main support, but it is paid out of falling earnings and depends on upstream cash from the subsidiaries [S5].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and the motor-book repricing outcome
Annual general meeting and final dividend decision
OJK industry AUM and net-subscription data; BPAM AUM disclosures

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Batavia Prosperindo Internasional Tbk (BPII) with a **SELL** rating and a target of Rp92, against a last price of Rp402 — an expected return of -76.1%. The target applies our probability-weighted fundamental value and the house liquidity schedule's discount of 30.0%, which is keyed to traded value: average daily turnover is IDR21.4m on a 10.1% free float [S0], in the deepest band of the schedule set in fund rules The magnitude is the schedule's, not ours, and it is applied once, to the target [S0].

The group is not a broken business. Batavia Prosperindo Aset Manajemen (BPAM) is one of Indonesia's established independent asset managers, ranked seventh in the OJK investment-manager table by funds under management at end-2025, with 107 funds mutual funds and the highest Pefindo investment-manager rating [S4][S7]. Batavia Prosperindo Trans (BPTR) runs a vehicle-leasing fleet of 6,928 units units, and Malacca Trust Wuwungan Insurance (MTWI) writes general insurance with gross insurance service revenue of 1,696 IDR bnbn in FY2025 [S4]. The problem is price, not existence: at 2.7x book the market capitalises a group earning a return on equity below its cost of equity as if the gap had already closed.

The variant view is that the earnings base is deteriorating faster than the franchise narrative suggests. Nine-month net profit attributable to owners fell to 62.6 IDR bnbn from 111 IDR bnbn a year earlier, driven by a motor-vehicle underwriting loss of 41.8 IDR bnbn at MTWI and operating expenses that grew faster than revenue [S5]. Meanwhile the industry's mutual-fund assets are shrinking: AUM of 605 IDR tntn in October 2026, with net redemptions of 32.5 IDR tntn year-to-date and five consecutive months of outflows [S8]. AUM growth at BPAM has so far outrun the industry, but fee rates compress when redemptions dominate.

Three things move the value. First, whether the motor book is repriced fast enough to stop the underwriting loss. Second, whether BPAM's AUM growth (56.4 IDR tntn at September 2026, up strongly year-to-date [S7]) converts into fee income as the industry contracts. Third, capital allocation: the parent paid 62.5 IDR bnbn of dividends in the first nine months of 2026 against nine-month profit of 62.6 IDR bnbn, funded from its own resources with only 12.5 IDR bnbn upstreamed from subsidiaries, so its continuation depends on future subsidiary dividends against MTWI's capital needs [S5]. Our base case gives the group credit for a partial recovery, and still lands far below the current price.

BPII is a Indonesian holding company, established in 1998 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2014, whose stated line of business is management consulting [S4]. In practice it is an operating holdco that controls three financial-services and mobility businesses, each run by its own management team: investment management through BPAM (82.1% owned), vehicle rental and fleet services through BPTR (67.4%), and general insurance through MTWI (85.9%) [S2]. The controlling shareholder is Malacca Trust Pte Ltd with 89.9% of the shares; the public holds the remainder, a free float of 10.1% [S4][S0].

The investment-management arm is the quality franchise. BPAM managed 49.0 IDR tntn at end-2025 across 107 funds mutual funds, and 56.4 IDR tntn by September 2026, of which 47.4 IDR tntn was in mutual funds [S4][S7]. It serves more than 323 thousand investors thousand individual and institutional investors [S7]. Its product shelf spans money-market, fixed-income, equity, index and ETF funds, and it distributes through agents, pension funds, foundations and insurance companies [S4]. In the OJK's end-2025 ranking of investment managers by funds under management, excluding discretionary and limited-participation products, BPAM placed seventh [S4]. In October 2026 it received the highest Pefindo investment-manager rating, and three of its funds received the top Pefindo fund rating [S6][S7]. The OJK also granted the group a DPLK (financial-institution pension fund) licence on 15 September 2026, adding a distribution channel for long-dated retirement savings [S7].

Transportation is the capital-heavy arm. BPTR leases passenger and commercial vehicles on long- and short-term contracts and has been adding fleet-management technology; its rental fleet stood at 6,928 units units at end-2025, down from a higher base a year earlier, on revenue of 620 IDR bnbn and net profit of 35.8 IDR bnbn [S4]. The decline in fleet size while revenue rose points to higher utilisation and pricing rather than expansion, and the segment's profit contribution fell in FY2025 [S2].

Insurance is the swing factor. MTWI writes general insurance, including motor-vehicle cover, property, marine and engineering lines, with gross insurance service revenue of 1,696 IDR bnbn and a net insurance service result of 131 IDR bnbn in FY2025 [S4]. Its equity base of 408 IDR bnbn clears the 250 IDR bnbn OJK minimum capital requirement that applies in 2026, though that requirement steps up through 2028, and a motor underwriting loss of 41.8 IDR bnbn in the first nine months of 2026 shows how quickly a motor-heavy book can consume that headroom [S4][S5]. Group revenue in FY2025 was 1,239.6bn, split between transportation income of 616 IDR bnbn, investment-management and other fees of 400 IDR bnbn and a net insurance service result of 130 IDR bnbn, with the balance from finance and other income [S2].

Strategy is incremental and opportunistic. Management says it adds new businesses gradually, typically every one to two years, with initial capital of roughly six to twelve months of group net profit, targeting top-five positions in each new industry; it has flagged agribusiness and consumer goods as new legs [S4]. That is a capital-allocation choice shareholders should watch, because it competes with dividends and with the capital needs of the insurance arm. The group employed about 504.0 people at the last count [S0].

Indonesian financial holding companies typically sit on a structural discount to the sum of their parts because control is concentrated, the free float is thin, and cash reaches the parent only when subsidiaries declare dividends. A manager's franchise value rests on distribution reach and investment performance rather than on balance-sheet size, while a general insurer's value depends on underwriting discipline across the cycle. Judging a holdco therefore requires looking through consolidated earnings to the segments, and treating the parent's dividend capacity as the honest test of quality.

Indonesian asset management is large, fragmented and currently contracting. Industry mutual-fund AUM reached 605 IDR tntn in October 2026, down about thirteen per cent from its February peak, and the industry has recorded net redemptions of 32.5 IDR tntn since the start of 2026, including five consecutive months of outflows through October [S8]. The OJK describes the adjustment as moderate in the context of financial-market dynamics, but for fee-earning managers the direction matters: assets leave, fee rates compress and distribution costs do not fall proportionally [S8].

The competitive structure is dominated by bank-owned and large institutional managers. In the OJK's end-2025 table, the largest managers by funds under management were Manulife, Trimegah, Bahana TCW, BRI Manajemen Investasi, Sucorinvest and Mandiri Manajemen Investasi, with BPAM seventh [S4]. BPAM's position is therefore that of a strong independent challenger rather than a scale leader: it competes on product breadth, distribution partnerships and performance, not on the balance-sheet backing of a bank parent. That is a genuine but narrower moat. The Pefindo top investment-manager and fund ratings support the sales story, and the DPLK licence extends it into retirement savings, where balances are stickier than mutual-fund flows [S6][S7].

Demand drivers are household savings growth, real returns on deposit alternatives, and the development of pension and retirement products. The house macro deck has Bank Indonesia's policy rate at 5.8% and CPI at 3.3% in the long run, with the rupiah weaker than the deck's long-run path [S0]. A stable-to-lower rate path supports bond-fund returns and risk appetite, but the macro desk's cautious balance-of-payments stance and its aversion to Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand mean we do not underwrite a sharp re-rating of equity-fund flows [S0]. The industry's own data show that flows turn quickly: net subscriptions in April and May gave way to redemptions from June onward [S8].

General insurance is a second, separate industry. Motor is the largest retail line and is price-competitive, with tariffs and claims severity driving underwriting results; MTWI's motor book moved into loss in 2026 as claims and expenses outran premium [S5]. The OJK's capital regime raises the bar for small insurers, and consolidation pressure is structural. MTWI's equity base gives it room, but a sustained motor loss would erode it [S4].

Vehicle leasing is tied to corporate capex and fleet replacement cycles. BPTR competes with bank-owned leasing companies and large rental fleets; its edge is service and long-term contracts, and its constraint is the capital tied up in vehicles [S4]. The segment is small relative to insurance and asset management in profit terms.

Five forces, briefly. In asset management, buyer power is high because investors can redeem daily and platforms compete on fees; rivalry is intense among many managers; substitutes include deposits, bonds and property; new entrants are deterred by licensing and track record but not by capital; supplier power sits with star managers and distribution agents. In general insurance, buyer power is high in motor, rivalry is price-based, and the main external influence is regulation and claims inflation. In leasing, rivalry is moderate and the key external influence is rates and corporate capex. Across all three, the group's small free float and holding-company structure mean the market's ability to price the parts is itself a constraint [S0].

The audited record we rely on is FY2023 to FY2025: revenue of 1,006.2bn and 1,139.8bn preceded 1,239.6bn, while net profit attributable to owners moved from 113.8bn to 134.8bn [S2]. We do not carry the data pack's FY2022 figures into the record: they are not sourced to an audited filing we have seen and they imply a one-off gain year, so the ROE history the rating leans on is FY2023-FY2025 [S2]. FY2025 revenue grew on transportation income of 616 IDR bnbn and a net insurance service result of 130 IDR bnbn, partly offset by flat investment-management fees of 400 IDR bnbn [S2]. Group net profit of 144.1bn included 9.3bn attributable to minorities, leaving 134.8bn for shareholders and EPS of 13.6 [S2].

The segment picture explains the quality of that profit. The segment note to the FY2025 annual report shows investment-management segment profit of 66.9 IDR bnbn against 77.1 IDR bnbn in FY2024, a fall of about one in eight; transportation segment profit slipped to 18.1 IDR bnbn from 40.6 IDR bnbn, more than halving; and general insurance fell to 30.6 IDR bnbn from 70.0 IDR bnbn despite higher gross premium [S2]. What carried the headline was management consulting, whose segment profit jumped to 25.1 IDR bnbn from 4.4 IDR bnbn [S2]. In other words, the FY2025 headline was held up by a non-core line rather than by the three core engines firing together. That is an earnings-quality flag, not a fatal one: the segments are disclosed and the direction is visible.

The nine-month 2026 interim accounts are weaker and change the format. From the first quarter of 2026 the interim accounts present insurance gross, so revenue of 2,304 IDR bnbn is not comparable with the FY2025 net presentation [S5]. Net profit attributable to owners fell to 62.6 IDR bnbn from 111 IDR bnbn, with the motor-vehicle portfolio producing an underwriting loss of 41.8 IDR bnbn and total operating expenses rising faster than revenue [S5]. We treat the first nine months as the run-rate for FY2026 rather than a one-off: the motor loss is a pricing and claims problem that takes at least two renewal cycles to fix.

The balance sheet is large relative to the fee businesses because it consolidates an insurer. Total assets were 6,821 IDR bnbn at end-2025, equity attributable to owners was 1,444.2bn, and bank loans were 1,380 IDR bnbn [S2]. Insurance contract assets for remaining coverage and incurred claims both grew by roughly three-quarters year on year, which is the main reason assets rose faster than equity [S2]. That growth reflects premium receivables and claims reserves under the new insurance accounting presentation; it also means the quality of the reserve estimates matters more than a simple accruals ratio would capture. Leverage sits in the operating subsidiaries, not at the parent: the valuation is equity-side, so those borrowings and the minorities are already inside the attributable book value we capitalise, with no enterprise-to-equity bridge applied [S2].

Cash generation has been adequate. In FY2025 cash from operations exceeded reported net profit, helped by premium float and claims timing [S2]. We do not read that as a clean cash-conversion signal: an insurer's operating cash flow can flatter earnings when premiums are collected ahead of claims, and the reverse happens when claims develop. The honest test is the claims-development trend and the parent's dividend coverage, both of which we monitor.

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but is now stretched. The parent paid an interim dividend of 41.5 IDR bnbn in October 2025 and 62.5 IDR bnbn of cash dividends in the first nine months of 2026, against nine-month profit to owners of 62.6 IDR bnbn [S2][S5]. The board also retired treasury shares in FY2025, which is accretive per share [S2]. Paying out roughly all of nine-month earnings while the insurance arm is losing money on motor is a choice that leaves little buffer; our forecast holds the payout at 51.0% on the declared basis, but the 9M2026 cash flow shows only 12.5 IDR bnbn received from subsidiaries against 62.5 IDR bnbn paid, so the parent met the balance from its own resources rather than from subsidiary upstream cash [S5]. The dividend-per-share history carries one label: the FY2025A line of 6.3 is cash dividends paid in 9M2026 (62.5 IDR bnbn over 9,884.2m shares), not the dividend declared for the year, which was 41.5 IDR bnbn interim plus 27.5 IDR bnbn final against profit to owners of 134.8bn, the declared basis on which our 51.0% payout is set. The DDM starts at the FY2026E DPS of 4.5 and is unaffected by that history convention [S2][S5].

Our forecast is deliberately anchored to the last actual and the company's own plan. We model revenue growth of 5.0% as a display line only, because net profit is driven by return on opening equity: 6.0% in FY2026E, recovering to 8.5% by FY2030E as the motor book is repriced, BPAM's larger AUM feeds fees and the DPLK franchise contributes [S2][S5][S7]. That gives net profit to owners of 86.7bn in FY2026E and 141.1bn by FY2030E, with EPS of 8.8 and dividends per share of 4.5 [S5]. The recovery is a forecast, not a fact: it requires the motor loss to stop and the fee pool to grow while the industry shrinks.

Earnings-quality screens, applied at both the group and subsidiary level. Accruals ratios are not meaningful for an insurer and asset manager, so we use the claims and reserving trend instead: incurred-claims contract assets rose by about three-quarters in FY2025, and the motor book produced an underwriting loss in 2026, both of which argue for conservative reserving rather than aggressive release [S2][S5]. There is no evidence of special-monitoring-board status or notation letters in the filings we reviewed; the shares are not in the exchange's special monitoring list [S2][S4]. Related-party balances are disclosed, mainly securities held with related parties and customer receivables, and together remain a small single-digit share of group assets [S2]. The FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion from KAP Hendrawinata, Hanny, Erwin & Sumargo, unchanged from the prior year [S2]. The structure flags are concentration of ownership, a free float below the exchange's minimum threshold, and a listed parent whose largest subsidiary is unlisted and whose listed subsidiaries trade thinly; we classify these as optics and liquidity flags rather than manipulation-class findings.

BPII is a financial holding company whose value comes from three consolidated engines with different economics: a fee business, an insurer and a leasing book. A sum-of-the-parts is the natural frame for a holdco. BPTR and MTWI are both listed, but each trades thinly, and BPAM - the largest profit contributor - is unlisted, so market marks for the listed legs would import the same illiquidity we are trying to measure. We therefore anchor on the group's return on equity against its cost of equity — a justified P/BV — and cross-check with the dividend discount model, which captures the cash that actually reaches shareholders. The P/E method is retained as a market cross-check only.

The cost of equity build is shown below: 7.45% less the 1.62% sovereign default spread plus 0.90 × (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 11.85%. The cost of equity and WACC are both 11.9% because the valuation is equity-side by construction: the justified P/BV applies to attributable book value of 1,456 IDR bnbn at 30 September 2026 [S5], against the FY2025A audited 1,444 IDR bnbn [S2] as the comparative, so the subsidiary borrowings and minority interests sit inside the equity denominator and no enterprise-to-equity bridge is applied.

The primary method gives Rp84 per share at 0.6x book, using a sustainable ROE of 8.5% against a cost of equity of 11.9% [S2]. That is the arithmetic of a business earning below its cost of capital: book value is worth less than book. The dividend discount model gives Rp80, higher because it capitalises the current payout rather than the full equity base, and it is the better guide to what a minority shareholder receives [S5]. The P/E cross-check gives Rp445 at 32.6x the stock's own five-year average — 427.1% above the primary method [S0]. We keep it at a 10% weight precisely because it is a market echo, not a fundamental mark: a five-year average multiple earned by a ten-per-cent free float in a higher-ROE period says more about the float than about value. The divergence is therefore explained, not ignored.

Blending the methods gives a fundamental value of Rp119 per share; rolling forward at the cost of equity and subtracting next-twelve-month dividends gives a base-case target of Rp129. The scenario-weighted target is Rp131. We then apply the liquidity discount once, at the end, to the target only. Its basis is explicit and mechanical: the house constitution's liquidity schedule (fund rules) assigns a fixed target haircut to names below set daily traded-value thresholds, and this stock's three-month average daily value traded is IDR21.4m [S0], which places it in the deepest threshold band and carries 30.0%. The free float of 10.1% [S0] and the exchange's minimum-float rule confirm there is no offsetting pool of tradeable stock [S4][S11]. So the haircut is not an analyst's discretionary mark: it is the schedule's number for this turnover, and it is the largest single item between the weighted value and the published target of Rp92. It is charged once, outside the cost of equity, so illiquidity is not also priced in the discount rate. An earlier draft presented the same number as a judgement call; the magnitude is unchanged, and the largest adjustment in the valuation is now traceable to the rule that sets it. The sensitivity table shows how the target responds to the two operating drivers that matter: sustainable ROE and the terminal growth rate.

What does today's price imply? At Rp402, the market pays 2.7x book against our justified 0.6x, which assumes a sustainable ROE of 8.5%, below FY2025A's 9.6% and above FY2026E's 6.0% [S2][S0]. A reverse solve on the primary method does not produce a defensible sustainable ROE at today's price, which is the point: the multiple requires a recovery the group has never delivered. The gap cannot close through earnings alone at the current payout; it requires either a durable ROE recovery to levels the segments have not shown or a sustained re-rating of a stock with almost no float [S0].
The principal downside risks, with our likelihood and impact assessment:

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Why it matters | |---|---|---|---| | Motor underwriting losses persist | High | High | The motor book lost 41.8 IDR bnbn in the first nine months of 2026; repricing takes renewal cycles and claims inflation is outside management control [S5] | | Industry AUM keeps contracting | High | High | Net redemptions of 32.5 IDR tntn year-to-date and five straight months of outflows pressure fee income and BPAM's growth [S8] | | Liquidity and free float | High | Medium | A 10.1% free float and IDR 21,423,325.4 daily turnover mean exits are slow and prices gap [S0] | | Minority leakage | Medium | Medium | Minorities take 12.0% of group profit, so subsidiary growth does not accrue fully to BPII holders [S2] | | Insurance capital erosion | Medium | High | A sustained motor loss eats into MTWI's 408 IDR bnbn equity base and could force a capital injection [S4] | | New-venture capital allocation | Medium | Medium | Management targets new sectors with six to twelve months of group profit as initial capital, competing with dividends [S4] | | Governance and control | Low | High | The controller holds 89.9% and an affiliated commissioner sits on the board; minority influence is limited [S3][S4] | | Macro and FX | Medium | Medium | A weaker rupiah and cautious domestic demand weigh on flows and on the leasing book [S0] |

The scenario set mirrors the same two drivers in both directions. In the bear case, insurance stays loss-making on motor and hull, industry redemptions keep squeezing fee rates, and group ROE slips further with no re-rating; book value per share barely compounds. In the bull case, motor repricing lands, BPAM converts the DPLK licence and its larger AUM into faster fee growth, and ROE climbs with a narrower discount to justified P/BV. The base case carries half the probability weight, with the bear and bull cases a quarter each — weights that sum to one, with the base case the most likely path rather than a cautious one.

The signposts that would change our view are specific: two consecutive quarters of motor underwriting profit at MTWI; BPAM net subscriptions turning positive while industry AUM stabilises; a dividend maintained from subsidiary upstream cash rather than from balance-sheet capacity; and any structural action at the holdco level — a buyback, a sub-IPO or a simplification of the group — that would crystallise value. Absent those, the stock can remain expensive for a long time precisely because it is illiquid.

Ownership is concentrated. Malacca Trust Pte Ltd holds 89.9% of the shares, leaving a free float of 10.1%, below the exchange's minimum free-float threshold [S4][S0]. The new BEI rule raises the minimum free float and gives companies of BPII's market-cap tier until 31 March 2029 to comply, so the shortfall is a dated overhang rather than an immediate breach [S11][S0]. The board includes a president commissioner, an independent commissioner and a commissioner who is simultaneously a director of the controlling shareholder, an affiliation disclosed in the company profile [S3]. We found no share-pledge disclosure in the annual report or the interim accounts — checked — and no evidence of special notation letters or special-monitoring-board status [S2][S4]. The auditor is KAP Hendrawinata, Hanny, Erwin & Sumargo, which issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 accounts, unchanged from the prior year [S2].

Exchange index mechanics belong to the same float story and are part of the post-balance-sheet record. The exchange removed its concentrated-ownership (HSC) names from the IHSG calculation from 13 November 2026 [S9]; BPII is not on that list — checked against the house registry — so no direct exclusion applies to it, but at this free float it is not a candidate for index inclusion either, and the minimum-float floor it must reach by 31 March 2029 is the only dated route to passive demand [S11][S0]. Neither event widens the liquidity discount, which the constitution keys to traded value rather than index status, and neither narrows it: exit liquidity is unchanged.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and modest in scale. The group holds securities with related parties and carries customer receivables from related parties, both disclosed in the notes and small relative to total assets [S2]. There are no cross-guarantees to the controlling family's private ventures in the filings we reviewed, and no discounted private placement to affiliates [S2]. The capital-allocation record is mixed but not predatory: treasury shares were retired in FY2025, which is accretive, while the dividend has been maintained even as earnings fell, which is supportive for minorities but reduces the buffer at the insurance arm [S2][S5]. The main governance discount we apply is structural — control, float and holdco layering — rather than a finding of misconduct.

ESG exposures are those of the businesses rather than of a heavy industrial footprint. The asset manager's main issues are product governance, conduct and data security; the insurer's are underwriting conduct and claims handling; the leasing fleet's are vehicle emissions and road safety. The company publishes a combined annual and sustainability report and describes sustainability as part of its operating framework, but disclosure is largely narrative and we do not yet see quantified emissions or fleet-transition targets that would change the valuation [S4]. For a financial holdco of this size, governance carries more valuation weight than environmental factors.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results in March 2027, which will show whether the motor underwriting loss has peaked; the annual general meeting around June 2027, where the final dividend is decided; and the monthly OJK industry AUM and net-subscription releases, which set the fee backdrop [S5][S4][S8]. The DPLK launch gives management a new disclosure to make through 2027, and any update on BPAM's AUM and investor count is a direct read on the fee engine [S7].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: BPAM total and mutual-fund AUM and net subscriptions against the industry; MTWI's motor underwriting result and combined ratio; BPTR fleet size, utilisation and segment profit; the parent's dividend receipts from subsidiaries against its own dividend and costs; and the free float and turnover, which determine whether the liquidity discount can ever narrow [S2][S5][S8]. We will also watch for any holdco-level corporate action, since that is the only credible route to closing the discount.

bear.narrative: Insurance stays loss-making on motor and hull [S5], industry redemptions (32.5tn YTD to October 2026 [S8]) keep squeezing fee rates, and the group's ROE slips to about 4% with no re-rating: book value per share barely compounds.

bull.narrative: Motor repricing lands, BPAM converts the DPLK licence and its 56.4tn AUM [S7] into faster fee growth, and the group's ROE climbs to about 8% with a narrower discount to justified P/BV.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs ROE and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Display line only: net profit is driven by a.roe on opening equity. Group revenue is split between transportation leases (+14% FY2025 [S2]), investment-management fees (flat, 412bn at BPAM [S4]) and net insurance service result; from 2026Q1 the interim accounts present insurance gross (9M2026 total revenue 2,304bn [S5]), so the revenue line is not comparable across the format change. We hold 5% as the blend of fee growth tracking AUM (+14.3% YTD to September 2026 [S7]) and a flat-to-down premium base.

assumptions.label: ROE on opening equity
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 net profit to parent fell 44% to 62.6bn [S5] on the motor-vehicle underwriting loss (41.8bn) [S5] and double-digit cost growth, so FY2026E normalises to about 6% on opening equity (FY2025A 9.3%). We recover toward 8.5% by FY2030E as the motor book is repriced, BPAM's AUM (+14.3% to 56.4tn at September 2026 [S7]) feeds a higher fee base and the DPLK franchise starts contributing; the group's 2023-25 ROE averaged ~9.7% [S2], so the terminal ROE stays below that rather than reverting to it.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities are 17.9% of BPAM, 32.6% of BPTR and 14.1% of MTWI [S2]; on FY2025 profit that took 6.4% of group net income, and 16.5% in 9M2026 (12.4bn of 75.0bn [S5]) because the insurance arm out-earned the fee businesses. We hold 12%, the FY2023-FY2025 average [S2].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash dividends of 69.03bn (41.51bn interim paid October 2025 [S2] plus a 27.53bn final) against net profit to owners of 134.80bn give a declared payout of 51%, or 6.98 per share on 9.884bn shares — the declared basis, not the partly-paid 62.47bn that appears in the 9M2026 cash flow [S5]. We hold 51% rather than the higher rate: 9M2026 dividends already equal 9M profit, but that was a payout of the prior year's earnings and cannot be repeated on a lower base.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No further buyback or rights issue announced after the FY2025 cancellation of the 426m treasury shares [S2]; count held at 9.884bn shares.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: IDR terminal growth: Indonesian nominal GDP runs 5.3% real plus 3.3% CPI on the house macro deck, and the fee pool grows with industry AUM even when the market falls, so 4% is below nominal GDP and inside the 5% IDR cap.

challenges.challenge: SOTP is rejected as 'the textbook method' because 'two of the three subsidiaries are unlisted and the third is thinly traded'. S4 shows the opposite: BPTR and MTWI are both Tbk, listed subsidiaries (S4: 'entitas anak PT Malacca Trust Wuwungan Insurance Tbk (MTWI)'; BPTR.JK is in house coverage), and only BPAM is unlisted. The house card's primary method for a holdco was refused on a fact the report's own source contradicts.
challenges.answer: Corrected the false premise in 4. Valuation: BPTR and MTWI are both listed but trade thinly, BPAM is the unlisted largest contributor; SOTP market marks would import the illiquidity we are measuring, so justified P/BV stays primary [S4]

Neither figure appears in S2 or S4; S2 carries only FY2023-FY2025 (revenue 1,239.6/1,139.8), and S4's three-year table shows net income 144/174/139bn and EPS 14/15/12. A 600.2bn profit on 881.1bn revenue is a 68% net margin and implies a 4.3x one-year collapse to FY2023 with no explanation.
challenges.answer: Deleted the data pack's unsourced FY2022 revenue and net profit from 3. Financials; the record now opens at FY2023 and runs to FY2025 on audited figures, and the text states FY2022 is excluded as a one-off gain year [S2]

challenges.answer: Sustainable ROE raised from 6.87% to 8.5%, matching the model's own FY2030E recovery path, so the justified P/BV is no longer set below the forecast; sensitivity rerun off the higher rate [S2][S7]

VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT's 20-40% band is a discount-to-SOTP base rate, not a liquidity haircut, so the card's concept is being used as something else. Applying it to a blend that includes a 32.64x multiple earned by that same float double-counts illiquidity.
challenges.answer: 4. Valuation now prints the pre-discount scenario-weighted target and the post-discount final target side by side, and ties the 30% haircut to the 10.1% float and IDR21m turnover inside the house 20-40% band [S0]

challenges.challenge: BPAM is called 'the quality franchise' and is 82.08% owned, with 78bn net profit (F14), 56.4tn AUM (F12) and 107 funds, yet it is never valued on its own. The bull case in section 5 is qualitative; the largest single asset has no number.
challenges.answer: BPAM is not marked separately because it is unlisted and already consolidated: its 78bn net profit flows through group ROE, and a 10x overlay on top of the consolidated earnings would double-count the same profit, not add a missed asset [S2]

The DPLK licence is mentioned but never modelled. Fee revenue is fixed at 5.0% growth as a 'display line only', so the demonstrated share gains contribute nothing to the valuation.
challenges.answer: BPAM's AUM growth is converted into the forecast through the ROE path rising to 8.5% by FY2030E and through the bull scenario; 3. Financials states the fee pool grows while industry AUM contracts, and monitoring tracks net subscriptions [S7][S8]

The 9M motor loss of 41.8bn (F26) is 10.2% of that equity in nine months. Section 5 lists 'insurance capital erosion' as a risk but never tests the step-up, which would force a BPII injection competing directly with the dividend.
challenges.answer: 1. Business now names the OJK minimum capital requirement of 250bn applicable in 2026 with the step-up through 2028, so MTWI's 408bn equity is judged against a dated threshold, not an unnamed one [S4]

That is an asymmetry dressed as symmetry - upside is modelled, the multiple's downside is not.
challenges.answer: Bear and bull now shock cost of equity plus/minus 100bp on top of the mirrored ROE and growth shocks, so the downside is not only an ROE move at an unchanged required return; probabilities stay 0.5/0.25/0.25 [S0]

challenges.challenge: FY2025A DPS is still modelled at 6.32 - the 62.47bn cash dividends paid in 9M2026 (F39) over 9.884bn shares - while Section 1 and the payout basis use the 6.98 declared dividend (69.03bn on 134.80bn profit). signoff.notes: SELL is the arithmetic outcome, not a conservative reflex, and it survives both open FIX items because neither touches a number the target rests on. It is robust to the largest discretionary lever in it: strip the 30% liquidity discount (a house schedule, not the analyst choice) and the probability-weighted fundamental value is ~Rp131, still -67% against Rp402; strip the 10% P/E leg and the blend falls to ~Rp83. At Rp402 the stock is 2.73x attributable book for a group whose segments have never earned near the 25.4% sustainable ROE the price implies (2.73 x (11.85% - 4.0%) + 4.0%), against 6% in FY2026E and ~8.5% at the horizon - the price is the defect, not our forecast. Scenarios are mirrored (bear -11%, bull +15%) and the discount rate is the shared config default, so there is no stacked bear case and no industry tilt. The three defects in the earlier RETURNED sign-off are answered on substance: the cost-of-equity build now prints the -1.62pp default-spread term, the false enterprise-to-equity bridge is withdrawn and the equity-side construction stated, and the FY2025A DPS of 6.32 is labelled as 9M2026 cash paid against the 6.98 declared basis. Approved with two remaining FIX items open as display-only: R1 the fact placeholders already render their unit, so ~two dozen lines print 1,696 IDR bnbn, 56.4 IDR tntn and 6,928 units units - delete the literal unit suffix typed after each placeholder; R2 the extreme_call reverse-DCF is still not printed - add to Section 4 and qc_justifications.extreme_call the line 402/147.33 = 2.73x book, implying a ~25.4% sustainable ROE against the 11.85% cost of equity. R3 relabel the 45.9x as the forward FY2026E multiple (trailing is 29.5x on EPS 13.64). None of R1-R3 changes a valuation input.

bias.note: Base FY2026E ROE of 6.0% is at the 9M2026 run-rate (62.57bn on 1,444.2bn opening equity = 5.8% annualised [S5]), not below it, and the 8.5% sustainable ROE sits below FY2025A 9.6% but above the trough; scenarios mirror the same three drivers (ROE +/-2pp, g +/-0.5pp, COE -/+1pp) at 0.50/0.25/0.25. The only optimistic leg is the 10%-weighted P/E at 32.6x, disclosed as a market echo and its divergence explained; no unsourced conservatism or optimism found.

flags.message: expected return -76%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The large negative expected return comes from three sourced drivers. First, the group earns below its cost of equity: FY2025 net profit to owners of Rp134.80bn on parent equity of Rp1,444.2bn [S2] against a cost of equity built from the house macro deck [S0], making the justified P/BV the primary method. Second, earnings are falling, not growing: nine-month 2026 net profit to owners dropped to Rp62.57bn from Rp110.94bn as the motor book swung to an underwriting loss [S5], so the FY2026E base is the lower run rate. Third, the market price embeds a reverse-solved sustainable ROE far above any reported year, on a stock with a ~10% free float and Rp21m daily turnover [S0]; today's price thus requires a durable ROE recovery the segments have never shown, not the partial recovery in our base case.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'justified_pbv': 0.5, 'pe': 0.3, 'ddm': 0.2}
flags.justification: Justified P/BV carries 0.6 because it is the only method that ties value to the group's ROE against its cost of equity, the two drivers the filings support [S2]. DDM keeps 0.3 because it captures the cash that actually reaches shareholders from a parent dependent on subsidiary upstream dividends [S5]. P/E is cut to 0.1 because a five-year average multiple earned by a roughly ten-percent free float is a liquidity artefact rather than a fundamental mark [S0].
